paper_role: candidate E6b interaction-level bridge; supports pairwise phenological response disparity but does not identify theoretical deadline costs

source.citation: Burgess MD et al. 2018. Tritrophic phenological match-mismatch in space and time. Nature Ecology & Evolution 2:970-975.
source.source_note: Published bivariate MCMCglmm analysis of UK oak-caterpillar-bird phenology; bird first-egg dates came from the BTO Nest Record Scheme and are not redistributed here.

estimand.definition: major-axis slope of higher-trophic-level phenology on lower-trophic-level phenology across years
estimand.interpretation: slope < 1 means the consumer shifts less among years than the resource, generating temporal variation in relative timing

interaction_pairs.pair: peak caterpillar biomass -> blue tit first egg date
peak caterpillar biomass -> great tit first egg date
peak caterpillar biomass -> pied flycatcher first egg date

licensed_interpretation: Across two independent published interaction settings, phenological response asymmetry among actual ecological partners translates into changing relative timing: bird-caterpillar mismatch increases in early springs, and resident-tit/migratory-flycatcher laying intervals diverge as their climate sensitivities differ. This supports response-asymmetry-to-mismatch, not a direct estimate of information-deadline difference.
not_licensed: the theoretical delay-cost difference D2-D1 has been measured
the q1 < q <= q2 asynchronous information-use window has been observed
information distance is the causal mechanism for the pairwise tracking deficits
pied flycatchers are more mismatched because of migration distance alone
the published Burgess pattern is a new PAYOFF-B discovery
the resident-migrant interval divergence identifies competition, social information, migration constraint, endogenous timing, or deadline costs as the causal mechanism

same_guild_resident_migrant_bridge.citation: Samplonius JM et al. 2018. Phenological sensitivity to climate change is higher in resident than in migrant bird populations among European cavity breeders. Global Change Biology 24:3780-3790.
same_guild_resident_migrant_bridge.design: 10 European nest-box schemes, 1991-2015, each with at least one resident tit species and one migratory flycatcher species
same_guild_resident_migrant_bridge.interaction_context: resident tits and migratory flycatchers overlap in nest-site competition, diet, and social-information ecology
same_guild_resident_migrant_bridge.published_interpretation: resident tits were about twice as temperature-sensitive as migratory flycatchers, and differential climate sensitivity was associated with increasing phenological separation
same_guild_resident_migrant_bridge.uncertainty_boundary: published source result only; PAYOFF-B does not reconstruct raw multi-site data or identify competition, social information, migration constraint, photoperiodic/endogenous control, or deadline costs as the causal pathway
